coredata.dc:description: Fluornen-9-bisphenol (BPFL) is used as one of the alternatives for bisphenol A. However, whether BPFL has deleterious effects to the male reproductive system and the underlying mechanism remain unknown. Here, we report the effects of BPFL on Leydig cell development in male rats in puberty. Male Sprague-Dawley (28 days old) rats were dosed with 0, 10, 100, 200 mg/kg/day BPFL via gavage for 28 days. BPFL significantly decreased serum testosterone levels at 200 mg/kg while increasing serum luteinizing hormone and follicle-stimulating hormone levels at 200 mg/kg. BPFL markedly increased Leydig cell number but down-regulated the expression of Cyp17a1 and its protein level in Leydig cells at 200 mg/kg. Further study showed that BPFL significantly increased Pcna and Cdk2 expression and increased Leydig cell proliferation at 200 mg/kg. BPFL treatment to immature Leydig cells isolated from 28-day-old male rats for 24 h significantly inhibited testosterone biosynthesis at 50 μM, which was completely reversed by the androgen receptor agonist 7α-methyl-nortestosterone and estrogen receptor α antagonist ICI 182,780. In conclusion, BPFL increases Leydig cell proliferation but inhibits its maturation in male rats in puberty by blocking androgen receptor and activating estrogen receptor α.

ce:abstract-sec.ce:simple-para: Fluornen-9-bisphenol (BPFL) is used as one of the alternatives for bisphenol A. However, whether BPFL has deleterious effects to the male reproductive system and the underlying mechanism remain unknown. Here, we report the effects of BPFL on Leydig cell development in male rats in puberty. Male Sprague-Dawley (28 days old) rats were dosed with 0, 10, 100, 200 mg/kg/day BPFL via gavage for 28 days. BPFL significantly decreased serum testosterone levels at 200 mg/kg while increasing serum luteinizing hormone and follicle-stimulating hormone levels at 200 mg/kg. BPFL markedly increased Leydig cell number but down-regulated the expression of Cyp17a1 and its protein level in Leydig cells at 200 mg/kg. Further study showed that BPFL significantly increased Pcna and Cdk2 expression and increased Leydig cell proliferation at 200 mg/kg. BPFL treatment to immature Leydig cells isolated from 28-day-old male rats for 24 h significantly inhibited testosterone biosynthesis at 50 μM, which was completely reversed by the androgen receptor agonist 7α-methyl-nortestosterone and estrogen receptor α antagonist ICI 182,780. In conclusion, BPFL increases Leydig cell proliferation but inhibits its maturation in male rats in puberty by blocking androgen receptor and activating estrogen receptor α.

Illustration of the working mechanism of bisphenol FL (BPFL)-mediated stimulation of Leydig cell proliferation and inhibition of Leydig cell maturation and in pubertal male rats.The androgen 7α-methyl-nortestosterone (MENT) binds the androgen receptor (NR3C4) in the cytoplasm, resulting in the formation of a ligand-receptor dimer and its translocation to the nucleus to transactivate the expression of NR3C4 target genes (Cyp17a1) upon binding AREs in the target gene promoter region. BPFL binds NR3C4 but does not form a dimer, thereby blocking NR3C4 transactivation. BPFL also binds ESR1 to transactivate the ESR1 activity to suppress the expression of steroidogenesis-related genes, thereby inhibiting T biosynthesis or increasing the expression of proliferation-related genes (Pcna and Cdk2) to stimulate the proliferation of immature Leydig cells (ILC).

ce:section.ce:para: Endocrine disruptors (EDs) are exogenous chemicals that interfere with endocrine-related receptors and biosynthesis of hormones. One such ED is the bisphenol A (BPA, Fig. 1 A), which is a synthetic material from which plastics and resins are made. BPA has been found to interact with the estrogen receptor α (ESR1) as an agonist [1] and the androgen receptor (NR3C4) as an antagonist [2]. Due to its widespread use and potential endocrine-disrupting effects, BPA has been restricted from manufacture and use in Europe and the United States [3]. The growing demand for alternatives of BPA has led to an increase in the use of BPA analogs. One of the BPA analogs is fluornen-9-bisphenol (BPFL, Fig. 1B). A recent survey for BPA analogs in seawater and organisms from the Pearl River Estuary in South China showed that BPA, bisphenol B, bisphenol S, bisphenol F, bisphenol B, bisphenol P, and BPFL had the median values of the logarithm of bioaccumulation factors (BAF) around 3.3–3.7, indicating that there is a bioaccumulation for BPA analogs including BPFL [4]. Epidemiological study in 353 people in Shenzhen city (China) showed that people in this area significantly exposed to BPFL with a mean serum level of BPFL of 0.578 ng/ml [5].

Although previous screening explorations have shown that BPFL and BPA are equally potent in binding to human ESR1 as weak agonists [6], the binding data have also shown that BPFL has an affinity for human NR3C4 about 600-fold higher than that of BPA and only about 9-fold lower than that of testosterone (T) [2], suggesting that BPFL can interfere with ESR1 and NR3C4 signal pathways. BPA has also been shown to weakly bind to G protein-coupled estrogen receptor 1 (GPER1) [7], which inhibited T production in rat and human Leydig cells [8], although there is no information for BPFL action on GPER1. Although some studies showed that BPFL can interfere with male and female reproductive systems, including the adverse effects on porcine Sertoli cells [9] and oocyte function [10] and mouse oocyte and ovarian function [11], the endocrine-disrupting toxicity of BPFL to Leydig cells is lacking.

Leydig cells are important cells in the testes that secrete testosterone to maintain male characteristics and to stimulate spermatogenesis (see review [12]). Previous studies have shown that puberty is a critical window for Leydig cell development and is controlled by pituitary hormones such as luteinizing hormone (LH) and follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH) and intratesticular factors [12]. Leydig cells secrete androgens, which autocrinely regulate via NR3C4 in immature Leydig cells and paracrinely regulate Leydig cell development via NR3C4 in Sertoli cells. NR3C4 deletion in Leydig cells [13] and Sertoli cells [14] and peritubular myoid cells [15] in mice resulted in delayed Leydig cell maturation. Interestingly, immature Leydig cells also secrete high amount of estradiol (E2) and express ESR1, and E2 can bind to ESR1 to stimulate immature Leydig cell proliferation and block Leydig cell maturation (see review [16]). In this study, we explored the effect of BPFL on Leydig cell development during puberty in male rats and dissected the underlying mechanism.

Materials and methods were described in detail in Supplementary Material S1. BPFL (CAS No. 3236-71-3; >97% purity) was purchased from Sigma-Aldrich (St. Louis, MO). ICI 182,780 (ICI) is an ESR1 antagonist [8], which was obtained from Zeneca Pharmaceuticals (Cheshire, UK), G15 is a GPER1 antagonist [17], which was obtained from MedChemExpress (Monmouth Junction, NJ), and 7α-methyl-nortestosterone (MENT) is an NR3C4 agonist [18], which was obtained from Upjohn (Kalamazoo, MI). Primer was appended in Supplementary Material S2. Antibody was listed in Supplementary Material S3.

Male Sprague-Dawley rats were purchased from Shanghai Laboratory Animal Center (Shanghai, China), which were 21 days old. Most reproductive data for BPA and its analogs were obtained from Sprague Dawley rats (see review [3]), therefore the Sprague-Dawley rat strain was selected. The rats were accustomed to the experimental environment for one week, and the environmental conditions were temperature of 21–25 °C, relative humidity of 45–55%, and day-night cycle (light: 09:00–21:00). This study was performed in accordance with the Guide for the Care and Use of Laboratory Animals and was approved by the Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee of Wenzhou Medical University. At 28 days, 32 rats were randomly assigned into 4 groups of 8 rats: 0, 10, 100, and 200 mg/kg BPFL. Although several low-dose BPA exposure studies in rodents found inhibition of Leydig cell function in animal models, the data remain controversial (see review) [3]. In this study, we used high doses of BPFL. Dose selection was based on previous reproductive studies for BPA and its analog bisphenol B for the comparison, in which both BPA and bisphenol B inhibited T secretion in male Sprague Dawley rats after exposure in puberty [19,20].

BPFL was dissolved in corn oil and orally administered daily to each male rat until postnatal day 56. Rats were euthanized on postnatal day 57. The exposure duration covers the developmental maturation of rat immature Leydig cells into adult Leydig cells in the late puberty [21]. Blood samples were collected 24 h after BPFL cessation for serum preparation. Serum was stored at −40 °C for T, LH, and FSH determination. Testes were collected for mRNA and protein assays. Caudal epididymis was collected for sperm counting.

Serum LH and FSH levels were measured by the commercial ELISA kits (Jianglai Industrial, Shanghai, China) as previously described [22]. A classic ELISA method using peroxidase-conjugated IgG anti-LH or anti-FSH antibody was performed. Finally the plate was read a by microplate read at a wavelength of 450 nm. LH or FSH was calculated by the standard curve method.

ce:section.ce:section-title: Counting sperm in the caudal epididymis
ce:section.ce:para: Sperm in the caudal epididymis was counted as previously described [23]. In brief, the whole epididymis was taken out and the cauda part was cut into small pieces in 2 ml PBS for sperm release. After incubation at 37 °C for 15 min, sperm suspension was mixed several times and a 0.5 ml sperm suspension was transferred to a corresponding test tube containing 2 ml PBS. The test tube was incubated at a 60 °C water bath for 1 min and cooled at room temperature. An aliquot of sperm suspension was loaded to a hemocytometer to count sperm and the total sperm in the whole cauda epididymis was calculated.

To measure a protein density at the same condition, testis tissue-array was prepared as previously described [22]. Briefly, after Bouin's solution fixation, each testis was set in a tissue array. The tissue was cut to 5 μm-thick sections. The sections were repaired in high-temperature and sealed with 10% goat serum. Then, sections were incubated with primary antibody of: 1) CYP11A1 (a Leydig cell biomarker) and SOX9 (a biomarker of Sertoli cells which number is stable after postnatal day 21) [24] for dual staining to count Leydig cell number; 2) CYP17A1 for CYP17A1 density in Leydig cells; 3) proliferating nuclear antigen (PCNA) staining for proliferation of Leydig cells. These slides were sealed and scanned by Nanozoomer-XR (Hamamatsu, Japan). The scanned image was displayed by Image-Pro-Plus 6 software and Leydig cell number, CYP17A1 density, and PCNA labeling was measured as previously described [22].

Testicular mRNA levels were measured by real-time quantitative polymerase chain reaction (qPCR) as previously described [22]. Total RNA was extracted from testis by Trizol Kit (Invitrogen, Carlsbad, CA) and its concentration as measured for OD at 260 nm. Reverse transcription kit (Vazyme Biotechnology, Nanjing, China) was used to prepare cDNA. The SYBR Green qPCR kit (Beyotime Biotechnology, Shanghai, China) was used to measure testicular mRNAs: 1) Leydig cell mRNAs (Lhcgr, Scarb1, Star, Cyp11a1, Hsd3b1, Cyp17a1, Hsd17b3, Srd5a1, Hsd11b1, Insl3, Chrna4, and Nr5a1), 2) Sertoli cell mRNAs (Fshr, Sox9, Dhh, and Pdgfa), 3) proliferation-related mRNAs (Pcna, Ccnd1, Cdk2, and Cdk4), 4) apoptosis-related mRNAs (Bcl2 and Bax), 5) antioxidant mRNAs (Sod1, Sod2, Cat, and Gpx1), 6) nuclear receptor mRNAs (Esr1 and Nr3c4), and 7) reference mRNAs (Rps16 and Gapdh). The standard curve of Ct value was prepared from the standards and mRNA levels were calculated. Because there were no changes for all reference mRNAs and Gapdh was finally used to normalize each target mRNA.

Testicular protein levels were measured by Western blot as previously described [22]. Briefly, testis was homogenized and lysed and the protein concentration was measured by BCA protein assay kit. The protein (30 μg) was denatured and electrophoresed. The following proteins STAR, CYP17A1, FSHR, PCNA, and CDK2 were measured using enhanced chemiluminescence kit and analyzed by Imagine Lab. The target protein was normalized to GAPDH, a housekeeping protein.

ce:section.ce:section-title: Purification and culture of immature Leydig cells
ce:section.ce:para: To explore the mechanism of BPFL, immature Leydig cells were isolated from 28-day-old male Sprague-Dawley rats as previously described [25]. In brief, rats were euthanized by CO2 asphyxiation and testes were removed and perfused. The decapsulated testes were digested with collagenase D and Percoll gradient centrifugation was used to collect cells with a specific cell density of 1.070–1.088 g/ml. The purity of cells was evaluated by HSD3B1 with purity >95%. Immature Leydig cells were seeded in a 12-well culture plate with the cell density of 1 × 106 in DMEM-F12 medium. Cells were cultured with various concentrations of BPFL (0, 1, 10, and 50 μM), ESR1 antagonist ICI (100 nM, which can significantly block ESR1 action without affecting Leydig cell steroidogenesis [8]), GPER1 antagonist G15 [17] (100 nM, which can significantly block GPER1 activity [26]) or specific NR3C4 agonist MENT (100 nM,which can stimulate Leydig cell steroidogenesis [27]) alone or BPFL (0, 1, 10, and 50 μM) in combination with ICI (100 nM) or MENT (100 nM) for 24 h. After 24 h treatment, medium was collected for measurement of testosterone in medium.

ce:section.ce:section-title: Measurement of serum and medium testosterone levels by HPLC–MS/MS
ce:section.ce:para: Serum and medium testosterone levels were determined by an Acquity ultra-high performance HPLC and the XEVO TQD triple quadrupole mass spectrometer (Waters Co., Milford, MA) as previously described [28]. Briefly, the testosterone-d5 internal control (10 μl) was placed to 100 μl serum or culture medium, and mixed with 200 μl acetonitrile, and centrifuged at 12,000×g for 15 min. The acetonitrile supernatant (1 μl) was automatically injected into the HPLC-MS/MS system for measurement. The intra-assay and inter-assay coefficient of variation of testosterone was less than 15%.

ce:section.ce:section-title: Measurement of serum BPFL levels by HPLC–MS/MS
ce:section.ce:para: Serum samples were collected 24 h after the last dose of BPFL. Serum BPFL levels were determined by an Acquity ultra-high performance HPLC I-Class system and the XEVO TQ-S triple quadrupole tandem mass spectrometer (Waters Co., Milford, MA) as previously described with a modification [29]. Mass spectrometric parameters were: desolvation gas 1000 L/h, capillary voltage 2.0 kV, cone gas 150 L/h, desolvation temperature 600 °C and collision gas 0.15 mL/min. The autosampler for analyzing samples was at 10 °C, along with 40 °C for the temperature of the column. 100 μl serum was mixed with 200 μl acetonitrile, and centrifuged at 12,000×g for 15 min. The acetonitrile supernatant (10 μl) was automatically injected into the HPLC-MS/MS system for measurement. Serum samples were collected 24 h after BPFL.

All date were shown as mean ± standard error (SEM). One-way ANOVA was used to analyze statistical significance, followed by post hoc Dunnett's multiple comparisons to the control. For Western blot analysis between samples, a paired Student t-test was performed, followed by Sidak adjustment. Statistical analysis was performed using GraphPad Prism (version 8, GraphPad Software Inc., San Diego, CA). p < 0.05 was considered statistically significant.

To investigate the impact of BPFL on Leydig cell development in pubertal male rats, BPFL was dosed via gavage to rats from 28 to 56 days postpartum. One rat in the control group and one rat in the 100 mg/kg BPFL group died due to accidental administration, which was confirmed by autopsy. After BPFL exposure, body weight, testis weight, relative testis weight, epididymal weight, and relative epididymal weight were without changes when compared to the control values (Table 1 ). There was no overt toxicity of BPFL in rats. We measured serum BPFL levels and found that BPFL dose-dependently increased serum BPFL levels of 12.55 ± 1.96, 70.45 ± 7.79, and 155.7 ± 29.62 ng/ml for 10, 100, and 200 mg/kg, respectively, 24 h after the last dose of BPFL.

ce:section.ce:section-title: BPFL decreases serum testosterone levels and lowers sperm number in the caudal epididymis
ce:section.ce:para: Serum testosterone, LH, and FSH levels were measured and it was found that BPFL significantly decreased serum testosterone levels at 200 mg/kg (Fig. 1D), while it significantly elevated serum LH (Fig. 1E) and FSH (Fig. 1F) levels at 200 mg/kg. BPFL markedly reduced sperm number in the caudal epididymis at 100 and 200 mg/kg (Fig. 1G). These data indicate that BPFL significantly delays Leydig cell development, as shown by a decrease in testosterone levels and a subsequent decrease in spermatogenesis.

ce:section.ce:section-title: Leydig cell number and proliferation is increased by BPFL
Leydig and Sertoli cell gene expression is altered by BPFL
ce:section.ce:para: We measured the transcript levels of Leydig cell genes (Lhcgr, Scarb1, Star, Cyp11a1, Hsd3b1, Cyp17a1, Hsd17b3, Srd5a1, Hsd11b1, Insl3, Chrna4, and Nr5a1) and Sertoli cell genes (Fshr, Sox9, Dhh, and Pdgfa). The data showed that BPFL significantly down-regulated the expression of Cyp17a1 at 100 and 200 mg/kg while up-regulating the expression of Fshr at 100 and 200 mg/kg (Fig. 4 ). Since the Leydig cell number is altered, we recalculated the transcript levels of Leydig cell genes after adjusting to Leydig cell number. It was found that the transcript levels of Scarb1, Star, Cyp11a1, Cyp17a1, and Chrna4 were significantly reduced by BPFL at 10–200 mg/kg (Fig. S1). This indicates that BPFL delays Leydig cell maturation by down-regulating the expression of some Leydig cell genes per se.

ce:section.ce:section-title: Leydig and Sertoli cell protein levels are altered by BPFL
BPFL alters the expression of signaling genes and their proteins
ce:section.ce:para: To investigate the underlying mechanism of BPFL, we chose several signaling pathways, including the proliferation-related genes (Pcna, Ccnd1, Cdk2, and Cdk4), pro-apoptotic gene (Bax) and anti-apoptotic gene (Bcl2), the antioxidant defense system (Sod1, Sod2, Cat, and Gpx1), and nuclear receptor genes (Esr1 and Nr3c4) and analyzed them by qPCR. The expression of Pcna, Cdk2, and Bcl2 at 200 mg/kg was significantly upregulated while the expression of other genes was not changed (Fig. 7 ). Further Western blot showed that PCNA and CDK2 levels were also increased in the 200 mg/kg BPFL group. These indicate that BPFL increases the cell cycle progression and survival.

ce:section.ce:section-title: BPFL decreases testosterone secretion by immature Leydig cells in vitro
ce:section.ce:para: Previous studies indicate that BPFL was an ESR1 and GPER1 agonist, and NR3C4 antagonist [3]. To further explore whether BPFL directly inhibited testosterone biosynthesis by immature Leydig cells, we measured testosterone output by immature Leydig cells after BPFL treatment alone or in combination with ESR1 specific antagonist ICI, GPER1 specific antagonist G15, and NR3C4 specific agonist MENT. As shown in Fig. 8 A, without the presence of ICI, BPFL significantly decreased testosterone output at 50 μM and ICI alone can increase testosterone output while BPFL in the combination of ICI did not cause the reduction of testosterone output, indicating that BPFL can act as an ESR1 agonist to inhibit testosterone production. As shown in Fig. 8B, without the presence of G15, BPEL significantly decreased testosterone output in 50 μM and G15 alone did not affect testosterone output and it cannot antagonize BPFL-mediated suppression of testosterone, indicating that BPFL exerts its inhibitory effects on testosterone production not through GPER1 signaling pathway. As shown in Fig. 8C, without the presence of MENT, BPFL significantly decreased testosterone output in 50 μM and MENT alone can increase testosterone output while BPFL in the combination of MENT did not cause the reduction of testosterone levels, indicating that BPFL can act as an NR3C4 antagonist to inhibit testosterone production.

This study shows that BPFL increases Leydig cell number and significantly reduces serum testosterone levels during puberty. This may be caused by its binding to NR3C4 as an antagonist or ESR1 as an agonist.

BPFL significantly stimulated Leydig cell proliferation as indicated by an increase in PCNA labeling in interstitial cells (Fig. 3), thereby increasing Leydig cell number at 200 mg/kg (Fig. 2). Apparently, this was due to increased expression of Cdk2 and Bcl2, which increased cell proliferation and survival [20]. Many exogenous factors can stimulate cell proliferation by increasing the expression of CCND1 and its partners CDK2, CDK4, and CDK6 [30]. In the present study, we did not find changes in CCND1, CDK4 and CDK6, but we found that CDK2 was significantly elevated after BPFL exposure. This increased CDK2 may promote cell progression as shown by increased PCNA expression in Leydig cells (Figs. 3 and 7).

Compared to the effect of BPFL on Leydig cell number, we found that BPFL significantly reduced serum testosterone levels by 200 mg/kg after 28 days of exposure (Fig. 1). The most sensitive gene was Cyp17a1, which was significantly down-regulated by BPFL (Fig. 4). To dissect whether increased Leydig cell number can mask the expression of other steroidogenic genes, we adjusted expression levels of Leydig cell genes to Leydig cell number. The expression of Scarb1, Star, Cyp11a1, and Cyp17a1 after adjusting for Leydig cell number was also significantly down-regulated (Fig. S1). This suggests that the maturation of the Leydig cells is delayed by BPFL exposure. Since STAR (a critical regulator for cholesterol transporting into inner membrane of mitochondria) is the rate-limiting step [31], the down-regulation of Star and its protein STAR may be related to the reduction of testosterone secretion.

The reduced androgen biosynthesis in Leydig cells and reduced serum testosterone level after chronic BPFL exposure led to increased pituitary LH secretion (Fig. 1). Increased serum LH levels in BPFL-treated rats possibly result from reduced sensitivity to androgen-mediated negative feedback on the hypothalamus and pituitary and the consequent stimulation of LH secretion. Our previous study using another BPA analog bisphenol B for similar exposure and found that bisphenol B can significantly reduce serum LH and FSH levels at 50–200 mg/kg/d [20]. This discrepancy may be due to the different binding affinity towards ESR1 and NR3C4. The negative regulation of pituitary gonadotropin LH secretion is exerted through the ESR1 in the pituitary cells and the feedback of serum testosterone [32]. As reported in the previous study [2], BPFL binds to human ESR1 with a potency of 0.8 relative to BPA while BPB binds to ESR1 with a potency of 9.1 relative to BPA, indicating that BPB is more potent ESR1 agonist than BPFL. That may explain why BPB can significantly reduce the secretion of LH and FSH. While the weak ESR1 agonism by BPFL cannot reverse the negative feedback effects due to the reduction of androgen by BPFL, which may be due to the most potent effects of BPFL binding to NR3C4 as an antagonist.

Decreased testosterone levels may also lead to decreased spermatogenesis. In fact, sperm count in the caudal epididymis was significantly reduced after BPFL exposure (Fig. 1). Elevated serum FSH levels further confirmed the arrest of spermatogenesis, which may be due to negative feedback to the hypothalamus and pituitary and consequent stimulation of FSH secretion.

The underlying mechanism of BPFL-mediated stimulation of immature Leydig cell proliferation and suppression of Leydig cell maturation may be related to its binding of ESR1 as an agonist and NR3C4 as an antagonist. Indeed, BPFL has comparable potency of human ESR1 binding to BPA as weak agonists [6].

ESR1 exists in Leydig cells of rats, and Leydig cell can synthesize E2 (see review [33]). Previous studies have shown that E2 can stimulate Leydig cell tumor cell proliferation through ESR1 [34], which may explain the increased Leydig cell proliferation. However, we cannot rule out an effect of elevated LH on Leydig cell proliferation, as LH is also a hormone that stimulates Leydig cell proliferation and survival [35]. In fact, previous studies showed that BPA also increased the proliferation of Leydig cell cells during puberty [36].

In addition to its proliferative effects, ESR1 is a negative regulator of Leydig cell maturation, and deletion of ESR1 significantly increased testosterone synthesis and Leydig cell hyperplasia [37]. In this study, in vitro treatment of ESR1 antagonist ICI can reverse the inhibitory effect of BPFL on testosterone production by primary immature Leydig cells (Fig. 8).

It is interesting that in mice BPFL can exert antagonistic effects of ESR1 [38], although its antagonistic effects of ESR1 in rats has not been reported. Previous studies showed that E2 or weak estrogens like BPA can directly inhibit testosterone production via ESR1 in rat Leydig cells [32,39,40]. If BPFL can exert antagonistic effects of ESR1 in rats, it should increase testosterone production by Leydig cells, which was not observed by our in vitro study (Fig. 8). Instead, BPFL can significantly inhibit testosterone production by rat Leydig cells in vitro and ESR1 antagonist ICI can antagonize BPFL-mediated suppression of testosterone production in Leydig cells, suggesting that BPFL acts as an ESR1 agonist like it does to human ESR1.

Previous studies showed that BPA and its analogs can bind to GPER1 receptor to exert effects [3] and GPER1 played a negative role in Leydig cell steroidogenesis [8]. We tested whether GPER1 antagonist G15 can reverse BPFL-mediated suppression of testosterone biosynthesis in vitro and found that G15 cannot antagonize BPFL-mediated suppression of testosterone output by primary Leydig cells (Fig. 8C). These indicate that GPER1 is not involved in BPFL-mediated action in Leydig cells.

Besides as an ESR1 and GPER1 agonist, BPFL also has high potency to bind to NR3C4, which is 600-fold more potent than BPA as an antagonist [2]. Previous studies have shown that NR3C4 plays a critical role in Leydig cell development through an autocrine mechanism. Deletion of NR3C4 in Leydig cells significantly delayed the maturation of Leydig cells by down-regulating the expression of many steroidogenic enzymes especially Cyp17a1 [13,41]. Indeed, androgen is a stimulator of immature Leydig cell steroidogenesis, which specifically up-regulated the expression of Cyp17a1 [42]. In this study, MENT, a potent NR3C4 agonist, can significantly stimulate testosterone production of immature Leydig cells, confirming the finding in the previous observation [42]. MENT also completely reversed BPFL-mediated suppression of testosterone by immature Leydig cells, further indicating that BPFL has an NR3C4 antagonistic mechanism. However, in the in vitro study, we used higher BPFL concentrations, we should carefully compare the in vitro findings with the in vivo finding.

Besides the autocrine mechanism, BPFL may also bind to NR3C4 in Sertoli cells to exert paracrine stimulatory effects. The deletion of NR3C4 in Sertoli cells of mice can significantly delay the maturation of Leydig cells [43], suggesting that BPFL can also bind to NR3C4 as an antagonist to block its signaling in Sertoli cells.

Due to the presence of different types of estrogen receptors, ESR1, ESR2, GPER1 (also called GPR30), and estrogen-related receptors (ERR α, β, γ) in Leydig cells [16,44], bisphenol-mediated actions become more complex. To complicate matters, some bisphenol analogs can act as ESR1 agonists or antagonists, such as BPFL, depending on the dose [38]. Therefore, the effects of BPFL may be contributed by many related mechanisms. Dissecting the detailed mechanisms of BPFL-mediated effects in different cell types is worthy investigating.

The inhibitory effect of BPFL on T levels in vivo occurred at a dose of 200 mg/kg/d, and the average serum BPFL level in rats was as high as 155.7 ng/ml (444 nM) 24 h after BPFL withdrawal, and its serum level was 368 times higher than the average serum BPFL level in the humans (0.423 ng/ml, equivalent to 1.21 nM) [5]. Although there are no pharmacokinetics data for BPFL in rats, we found that 24 h after the last dose of BPFL, high serum BPFL levels were still detected, indicating an accumulation of BPFL in rats. The in vitro inhibitory effects of BPFL on testosterone output by Leydig cells occurred at 50 μM, which was also much higher than the serum BPFL level in the humans. Therefore, the reproductive toxicity generated by both in vivo and in vitro studies should be carefully declared. However, for BPFL-manufacturing workers, serum levels of BPFL may increase several-fold. In this particular case, BPFL exposure should be of concern. Interestingly, several studies using low dosed pg BPA (μg/kg/d body weight range) also produced inhibitory effects on Leydig cell function (see review [3]). Whether low-dose BPFL can generate similar effects to low-dose BPA requires further investigation.

There is an increased detection rate of BPFL in humans [45]. However, its toxicity, especially the epidemiological data, is largely lacking. The establishment of the association between BPFL and reproductive system parameters remains to be investigated.

We demonstrate that BPFL inhibits testosterone biosynthesis by down-regulating some key steroidogenesis-related genes, such as Scarb1, Star, Cyp11a1, and Cyp17a1, in Leydig cells per se. This inhibition may be due to its binding to estrogen receptor α (ESR1) as an agonist and to the androgen receptor (NR3C4) as an antagonist, since the potent androgen MENT and ESR1 antagonist ICI can reverse its effect of BPFL on testosterone output. Stimulation of ESR1 by BPFL may also lead to increased expression of Cdk2, which stimulates the proliferation of immature Leydig cells. However, these effects of BPFL were found in the high doses, which were much higher than human serum BPFL level (see Graphic abstract).
